title: Cardiovascular Effects of Childhood Radiotherapy.
authors: Alexandra Khorasanchi; Jenna Farris; Taylor Choi; William H Frishman; Wilbert S Aronow
abstract: Cardiovascular disease is an important, well-studied late effect of childhood cancer therapy that may manifest many years after treatment. Radiotherapy, particularly when the heart is exposed, has been associated with multiple cardiovascular complications, including heart failure, coronary artery disease, valvular disease, and arrhythmias. This review examines the cardiovascular effects of radiotherapy in childhood and adolescent cancer survivors, with a focus on the mechanisms of radiation-induced injury, major cardiovascular outcomes, factors influencing long-term risk, and advances in cardiac-sparing radiotherapy and surveillance. The literature indicates radiotherapy was associated with an increased long-term risk of cardiovascular disease. Cardiovascular risk was influenced by radiation dose and the volume and location of cardiac tissue exposed, as well as age at treatment, anthracycline exposure, and traditional cardiovascular risk factors. Modern radiation techniques, including intensity-modulated and proton therapy, have aimed to reduce cardiac exposure. However, long-term clinical outcome data for these approaches remain limited. These findings support long-term cardiovascular surveillance of childhood cancer survivors and emphasize the importance of minimizing cardiac radiation exposure and addressing modifiable cardiovascular risk factors. Improved assessment of radiation dose to specific cardiac structures may further enable individualized risk stratification and surveillance.

title: Preconception Evaluation for Cardiovascular Disease: Who, What, and Why?
authors: Gianna Wilkie; Kevin O'Day
journal: Obstetrics and gynecology clinics of North America
abstract: Preconception counseling and evaluation for individuals with cardiovascular disease is essential to optimize maternal and fetal outcomes by identifying risk and stabilizing conditions before pregnancy. It should be offered to patients with structural heart disease, cardiomyopathies, arrhythmias, valvular disease, aortopathies, prior adverse pregnancy outcomes, or significant cardiovascular risk factors. Key components include risk stratification, targeted diagnostic testing, medication review, and counseling on pregnancy timing, expected course, and contraception when appropriate. This approach can reduce severe maternal morbidity, improve fetal outcomes, and enhance care coordination. Preconception evaluation enables informed decision-making and focuses care on prevention, improving pregnancy and long-term cardiovascular health.

title: Development and evaluation of X-ray lithophanes as test objects for interventional procedure simulation.
authors: Carlo Saija; Madeleine Dietrich; Federica Facente; Wen Wei; Campbell Littlefield; Mariia Kryshchuk; Pablo Aparicio-Villar; Nassim Boudjatit; Antonia Pontiki; Richard James Housden; Eric Sejor; Kawal Rhode; Pierre Berthet-Rayne
abstract:
In the growing field of interventional radiology, emerging technologies implement the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to help tackle growing demands for treatment. Due to the anatomical differences in animals, volunteers offer the most realistic training and testing scenario, however safety considerations restrict rapid prototyping of these new technologies. Simulators have been a key facilitator in the testing of new technologies among numerous medical engineering studies, but often lack the realism to reliably test AI.
This proof-of-concept study presents methods to create or enhance hyper-realistic radiographic simulators that can effectively function with a medical-grade AI software.
Iron-filled plastic was used to three-dimensionally (3D) print a series of blocks of heights up to 30 mm. By analyzing the intensities generated by different thicknesses of plastic, anonymous fluoroscopic images were turned into height maps (lithophanes) and 3D-printed. A static scene from transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) was then 3D-printed and imaged with different presets using two different x-ray systems for mathematical analysis. Lithophanes were then used as a radiographic background to experimental and commercial interventional simulators to test Caranx Medical's TAVIPILOT AI. Finally, fluoroscopies from 5 3D-printed lithophanes were mixed with 5 real images and presented to 5 expert volunteers to establish their realism in a structured survey.
The 3D-printed x-ray lithophanes test-plates' radiographic appearance was rated as "Adequate" to "Good" across all fields of the survey, with participants praising their realism. The test-plate was able to reliably recreate the TAVI scene in different x-ray systems, with joint-histogram correlation coefficients above 0.9, and global structural similarity above 0.8. The lithophanes were imaged as a standalone test plate and as a backing to dynamic TAVI interventional simulators; in both cases, TAVIPILOT AI responded to the simulator as if it was operating on a real anatomical image.
Lithophane plates present an easy-to-implement solution to recreate monoplane x-ray scenes, which can be deployed to test software at the point of care with minimal logistical, ethical, or safety concerns. This study opens the door for a new range of interventional simulators able to recreate human-like appearance to test AI, offering a non-exclusive alternative to patient volunteers and anonymous data.

title: LGS modified aortic valve reimplantation with neosinus creation for aortic root aneurysm.
authors: Luka Mitar; Lars Svensson
journal: Multimedia manual of cardiothoracic surgery : MMCTS
abstract: Valve-sparing aortic root replacement is an alternative to composite valve conduit replacement in patients with a morphologically preserved aortic valve and aortic root aneurysm or dilation. This video tutorial demonstrates a modified aortic valve reimplantation technique in which the aortic anulus is sized to the expected normal diameter for the patient's sex and body surface area, using a Hegar dilator as a sizing guide. The aortic valve is mobilized, and pledgeted sutures are passed from inside the left ventricular outflow tract through a straight polyester tube graft, then tied down around the appropriately sized Hegar dilator. This step reduces the annulus to a normal calibre and simultaneously creates neosinuses above the left ventricular outflow tract to accommodate cusp motion. The valve is sewn into the graft, commissures are resuspended as needed, and the neosinotubular junction is recreated by spacing the commissural sutures 4-5 mm apart. The coronary buttons are reimplanted, and the repair is completed with cardioplegia testing for valve competence. This technique has been used in over 500 patients with excellent mid- and long-term freedom from reintervention and low rates of residual aortic regurgitation.

title: Admission Albumin-Corrected Anion Gap and Subsequent Tricuspid Regurgitation Velocity Elevation After COPD Exacerbation.
authors: Zilin Zhao; Xiu Zhou; Xi Lu; Sang Zou
abstract: Admission albumin-corrected anion gap (ACAG) may reflect metabolic stress during an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD), but its relationship with subsequent pulmonary vascular abnormalities is unclear. This study included 294 adults hospitalized with AECOPD between January 2022 and November 2024 in a single-center retrospective cohort. Participants had baseline tricuspid regurgitation velocity (TRV) <3.4 m/s and at least one follow-up echocardiogram. The primary endpoint was first detected TRV ≥3.4 m/s within 12 calendar months after discharge. During available follow-up, 105 participants (35.7%) reached the endpoint and 12 died before detection. Each 5 mmol/L higher ACAG was associated with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.17 (95% CI, 1.51-3.11) and a cause-specific hazard ratio of 1.66 (95% CI, 1.34-2.05). A sensitivity analysis using TRV >3.4 m/s identified 99 events and gave an adjusted odds ratio of 1.90 (95% CI, 1.32-2.75). Adding ACAG to the clinical reference model increased the cross-validated area under the curve from 0.803 to 0.829; the extended-model calibration slope was 0.823. Among participants without a detected event, the last readable echocardiogram occurred a median of 323 days after discharge. Admission ACAG was associated with subsequent TRV elevation and provided modest additional discrimination in this cohort. Its availability in routine admission testing makes it a candidate for further evaluation in post-exacerbation risk assessment, with prospective external validation needed before clinical application.

title: Minimally invasive mitral surgery in patients with high pulmonary artery pressure: Results of a multicenter observational study.
authors: Silvia Mariani; Cristina Barbero; Valentina Gislao; Cecilia Capozza; Pierluigi Stefano; Paolo Centofanti; Vittoria Lodo; Francesco Onorati; Giorgia Cibin; Germano Di Credico; Andrea Audo; Ruggero De Paulis; Mauro Rinaldi; Giovanni Marchetto; Minimally Invasive Mitral Valve Surgery Registry Investigators
abstract:
Pulmonary hypertension is diagnosed in 40% to 75% of patients affected by mitral valve diseases. Little is known regarding outcomes of patients with pulmonary hypertension undergoing mitral valve oeprations through minimally invasive approaches. This study compares the characteristics and in-hospital outcomes of patients undergoing minimally invasive mitral valve surgery, stratified by systolic pulmonary artery pressure.
This multicenter, retrospective, prospective, observational study included adults undergoing mitral valve operations through a right minithoracotomy with or without tricuspid valve surgery and atrial fibrillation ablation between 2020 and 2024. Comparisons were performed between patients with systolic pulmonary artery pressure less than 31 mm Hg, systolic pulmonary artery pressure 31 to 55 mm Hg, and systolic pulmonary artery pressure more than 55 mm Hg based on European System for Cardiac Operative Risk Evaluation II cutoffs for systolic pulmonary artery pressure categories.
This analysis included 1121 patients (female, 47.5%; median age, 69 years, interquartile range, 59-77). Median systolic pulmonary artery pressure was 38 mm Hg (interquartile range, 30-50; systolic pulmonary artery pressure <31 mm Hg: n = 307, 27.4%; systolic pulmonary artery pressure 31-55 mm Hg: n = 152, 55.3%; systolic pulmonary artery pressure >55 mm Hg: n = 194, 17.3%). Patients with higher systolic pulmonary artery pressure were older, mainly female, and characterized by more comorbidities including atrial fibrillation and renal disease. A critical perioperative state was diagnosed in 12% of patients with systolic pulmonary artery pressure more than 55 mm Hg (P < .001). Patients with higher systolic pulmonary artery pressure more frequently underwent mitral valve replacement and tricuspid annuloplasty and experienced more postoperative dialysis and pacemaker implantation but comparable rates of conversions to sternotomy, respiratory and bleeding complications, and in-hospital mortality (systolic pulmonary artery pressure <31 mm Hg: n = 3, 1%; systolic pulmonary artery pressure 31-55 mm Hg: n = 6, 1%; systolic pulmonary artery pressure >55 mm Hg: n = 5, 2.6%; P = .222) compared with patients with lower systolic pulmonary artery pressure.
Despite a higher preoperative complexity, patients with high systolic pulmonary artery pressure could be considered for minimally invasive mitral valve surgery with acceptable rates of major intraoperative or postoperative complications regardless of their systolic pulmonary artery pressure values.

title: Association of haematologic parameters with persistent rheumatic heart disease stage in children: a pilot study.
authors: Nida Gülderen Kalay Şentürk; Sevim Aslı Ehlil; Ali Karakaş; Samed Cihad Çelik; Nergis Akay; Büşra Albayrak; Hazal Cansu Çulpan; İlker Kemal Yücel; Özgür Kasapçopur; Reyhan Dedeoğlu
abstract:
Rheumatic heart disease remains a major cause of cardiovascular morbidity in children. Although echocardiography is central to diagnosis and staging, it does not directly reflect inflammatory processes that may contribute to ongoing valvular damage. This study aimed to evaluate the association between baseline haematologic parameters and persistent rheumatic heart disease stage in children with prior acute rheumatic fever.
In this single-centre retrospective pilot study, 45 children with persistent rheumatic heart disease were classified as Stage A (n = 23), Stage B (n = 14), or Stage C (n = 8) according to the 2023 World Heart Federation echocardiographic staging framework. Baseline laboratory values obtained during acute presentation were analysed. Clinical and laboratory variables were compared across stages using non-parametric tests. Binary logistic regression identified factors associated with advanced disease (Stage B-C vs Stage A).
Markers reflecting acute inflammatory activity, including leukocyte counts and derived indices, did not differ significantly among stages. In contrast, red cell distribution width, mean platelet volume, and platelet distribution width differed significantly. In multivariable analysis, red cell distribution width, and mean platelet volume were independently associated with advanced persistent rheumatic heart disease stage, with higher values linked to increased odds of Stage B-C disease.
Red cell distribution width and mean platelet volume were associated with advanced stages of persistent paediatric rheumatic heart disease. These widely available haematologic markers may complement echocardiographic assessment. Larger prospective studies are needed to define their clinical utility.Trial registration: Not applicable (retrospective study).
