title: Practical Solutions to Common TAVI Complications
authors: Herbert Kroon
abstract: Aortic valve stenosis Calcific aortic valve degeneration mainly affects the elderly population. Approximately 15% of elderly patients have some degree of aortic stenosis (AS)1. Untreated severe AS will lead to heart failure, angina and/or syncope and approximately half of patients will expire within 2 years after symptom onset1, 2. Historically, open heart surgery was the only treatment for severe AS. However, advanced age was a dominant argument to defer surgery. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) was contrived as a less invasive alternative to surgery and to fulfill this unmet clinical need. After the first-in-human procedure in 2002, TAVI matured into a guideline recommended treatment of symptomatic severe AS in elderly patients across the entire risk spectrum3-7. Peri-procedural embolization Operator experience, improved planning and implantation strategies and multiple device iterations including smaller profile, repositioning ability and outer sealing fabric converted TAVI into a reproducible and relatively safe procedure8. However, the “Big Five” of complications in the modern TAVI era remain 1) access site complications and bleedings, 2) paravalvular leakage (PVL), 3) acute kidney injury (AKI), 4) conduction disturbances including the need for permanent pacemaker implantation (PPI) and 5) stroke9. Up to 5% of patients suffer a neurological event after TAVI, mainly within the first 48 hours8, 10, 11. This finding suggests a direct causative role with the transcatheter valve implantation itself. Transcranial Doppler and brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) studies revealed debris embolization towards the brain and new brain lesions after TAVI in the vast majority of patients12-15. Most of these embolizations remain clinically silent at first sight but may be linked to neurocognitive decline and frank dementia16. Embolic protection devices (EPD) have been developed to deflect or capture embolized debris on its way to the brain and may possibly reduce brain lesions and neurological events including stroke and neurocognitive decline. Part I of this thesis adds perspective to the etiopathology of TAVI related stroke and the mechanism of action of the current spectrum of cerebral embolic protection devices. We also present insights into the microscopic analysis of debris that was captured with filters during TAVI procedures. Vascular access and complications 1 TAVI typically requires large bore femoral artery access. By default, larger arteriotomies are at higher risk for access site complications and bleedings. A completely percutaneous approach relies on vascular access closure devices (VCD) to manage the arteriotomy and provide patent hemostasis. TAVI in low to intermediate risk patients is associated with a major vascular complication rate ranging between 2 and 8%4, 11. The conventional closure technique is based on sutures and most access site complications after TAVI procedures are related to closure device failure17. A collagen plug based closure device was introduced as an alternative to sutures. Part II of this thesis addresses vascular complications and provides information on clinical outcomes with collagen plug-based VCD. TAVI-related conduction disturbances Acquired conduction disturbances after TAVI are frequent and may lead to heart failure (re-) admissions and impaired long-term prognosis18-22. The atrioventricular bundle pierces the membranous septum between the right and non-coronary cusp of the aortic valve and surfaces along the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT), which makes it vulnerable to contact pressure by the implanted transcatheter heart valve (THV) during TAVI23, 24. New left bundle branch block (LBBB) and third-degree atrioventricular block (AV3B) requiring PPI occur in up to a third and quarter of patients, respectively18-22. These conduction disturbances may be transient or remain permanent which is clinically relevant in view of in-hospital stay and overall healthcare costs. Unfortunately, there are no uniform definitions to describe conduction dynamics post-TAVI. Inconsistent reporting makes the interpretation of the literature on this topic challenging. Part III of this thesis will elaborate on what is currently known about the incidence of newly acquired conduction disturbances after TAVI and studies specific features on the baseline and postprocedural electrocardiogram (ECG) to predict conduction dynamics. These insights may help determine the need and timing of PPI and adjust hospital discharge policies.

title: A rare cause of dysfunction of mechanical aortic valve prosthesis in a young adult
authors: Todor Dimitrov; Ивилин Тодоров
abstract: A mechanical prosthetic valve dysfunction carries a high risk of hospitalization and patient death. It may show up as stenosis of the valve prosthesis or intra/paraprosthetic regurgitation. Prosthetic stenosis, in turn, may be caused by granulation tissue (pannus), thrombosis, a combination of pannus and thrombosis, a prosthesis mechanical defect, or a unique surgical technique. Establishing the specific cause of prosthetic stenosis is of crucial importance for the therapeutic behavior. Prosthetic thrombosis requires conservative intensification of anticoagulation/fibrinolysis or surgical treatment in an accelerated/emergency manner. When the cause of the thrombosis is pannus, a mechanical defect, or surgical technique, the only treatment option is cardiac surgical reintervention. The manifestation of granulation tissue (pannus) is indicative of a non-immune reaction to the prosthetic valve and suture material following prosthetic valve replacement. The basis of this phenomenon is the growth of fibroelastic tissue associated with an increase in the expression of transforming growth factor beta. [1] In a small proportion of patients with implanted prosthetic valves, the growth of pannus leads to subvalvular obstruction of blood flow and results in prosthetic stenosis. Despite the technological advancements in imaging diagnostics, visualizing pannus remains challenging and not always feasible. Consequently, we employ a multifaceted approach that incorporates anamnestic, clinical, and imaging methods to reach a diagnosis. Operative exploration is the only method by which definitive confirmation can be obtained. The objective of this article was twofold: first, to present a rare case of stenosis of a mechanical aortic valve prosthesis due to a circumferential shaft of granulation tissue (pannus) forming a kind of de novo subaortic membrane; and second, to outline an algorithm for the diagnosis of prosthetic valve stenosis and differential diagnosis between thrombosis and pannus as the cause of valve dysfunction. The following case study presents a patient who met the surgical treatment indications due to stenosis of a mechanical aortic valve prosthesis. The clinical information and imaging studies indicated that the prosthetic dysfunction was likely due to the presence of granulation tissue (pannus). The intraoperative finding revealed a circumferential shaft of granulation tissue, forming a novel subaortic membrane.

title: Diastolic Dysfunction in Congenital Heart Disease: A Pressure-Volume Loop Analysis of Borderline Left Heart
authors: Nikhil M. Thatte; Martin Liberman; Peter E. Hammer; Ryan M. Callahan; Jesse J. Esch; Michael Farias; Gerald Ross Marx; Rebecca Sussanne Beroukhim; Eric N. Feins; Sitaram M. Emani; Sunil J. Ghelani
abstract: Abstract Background Diastolic dysfunction is a major driver of morbidity in congenital heart disease (CHD), but its mechanisms are poorly understood. It remains unknown whether left ventricular (LV) diastolic dysfunction in borderline left heart patients is caused by a defect in active relaxation or in passive compliance. Objectives We sought to apply gold-standard pressure-volume (PV) loop analysis to define the primary mechanism of diastolic dysfunction in patients with borderline LV (bLV). Methods We analyzed invasive PV loop data from pediatric patients with bLV (n =13) and a comparison group of patients with congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries (ccTGA, presumed no diastolic dysfunction; n=14). PV loops were generated during transient preload reduction and augmentation. Active relaxation was assessed by the isovolumic relaxation time-constant (τ) and maximal rate of pressure decline (dP/dt min ) indexed to peak-systolic pressure (PSP). Passive compliance was quantified by the chamber stiffness constant (β), derived from the multi-beat end-diastolic PV relationship (EDPVR). To account for size differences, β was (1) calculated using indexed ventricular volumes (iβ), and (2) converted to a dimensionless stiffness constant (β W ) by multiplying β by ventricular wall volume. Results Active relaxation measures were similar between groups, indicating normal lusitropy in bLV (τ bLV: 28 [23.5-29.5] vs ccTGA: 24 [21-28] msec, p=0.10; dP/dt min /PSP bLV: -10.6 [-11.0, -9.4] vs. ccTGA: -9.9 [-10.5, -8.7] s -1 , p=0.17). In contrast, patients with bLV had markedly abnormal passive compliance. The EDPVR was shifted sharply upward and to the left, and the stiffness constants were significantly higher in the bLV group (iβ bLV: 0.10 [0.04-0.35] vs. ccTGA: 0.03 [0.02-0.04] m 2 /mL, p=0.003); β W bLV: 4.08 [1.60-7.52] vs. ccTGA: 1.21 [0.95-1.77], p=0.002). Conclusions The primary mechanism of diastolic dysfunction in bLV is impaired passive ventricular compliance, and not impaired active relaxation. These findings suggest a limited role for lusitropic medications and therapeutic strategies that focus on mitigating ventricular stiffness (such as surgical endocardial fibroelastosis resection) may be more valuable. Condensed abstract Pressure-volume loop analysis with preload alteration in pediatric congenital heart disease shows that in borderline left heart patients left ventricular diastolic dysfunction is caused by impaired passive compliance, with preserved active relaxation. This mechanistic insight suggests that interventions targeting ventricular stiffness such as surgical endocardial fibroelastosis resection may be more beneficial than the use of lusitropic medications to improve outcomes.

title: Technical development and implementation of 3D‐QALAS on a 1.5T MR‐Linac for the brain: A prospective R‐IDEAL stage 0/1 technology development report
authors: Lucas B. McCullum; Ashley Harrington; Natalie A. West; Grace Nehring; Clifton D. Fuller; Ergys Subashi; Brian A. Taylor; Ken‐Pin Hwang; Clifton David Fuller
journal: Journal of Applied Clinical Medical Physics
abstract: BACKGROUND: Quantitative relaxometry of the brain on the integrated MRI / linear accelerator (MR-Linac) at high isotropic reconstructed resolution is currently limited due to prohibitively long scan times and limited field-of-views. PURPOSE: The purpose of this study was to assess the technical feasibility of the 3D-QALAS technique on the 1.5T MR-Linac which can acquire whole-brain 1 mm isotropic quantitative T1, T2, and PD maps along with multiple synthetic images in a 7-minute acquisition time. METHODS: A 1 mm isotropic 3D-QALAS acquisition was scanned in both phantoms and five healthy volunteers on the 1.5T Elekta Unity MR-Linac device with scan times around seven minutes. A test-retest protocol across five independent sessions for the phantom was conducted. The Lin's Concordance Correlation Coefficient (LCCC), repeatability, and reproducibility between measured and reference quantitative T1, T2, and PD values were determined in the phantom. Distortion was also studied. Vendor-provided reconstruction through SyMRI was performed to extract synthetic images and brain volume metric assessments in the healthy volunteers. RESULTS: The slope and LCCC between the measured and phantom reference values was 1.02 (1.00), 1.09 (0.90), and 0.99 (1.00) for T1, T2, and PD, respectively. Median distortion across the phantom remained below 2 mm. The repeatability and reproducibility coefficient-of-variation (CoV) was under 8% for all measured values. The measured brain volumes in the healthy volunteer was within expected age-adjusted reference values. CONCLUSIONS: The technical feasibility of using 3D-QALAS on the integrated 1.5T MR-Linac was confirmed. Applying this technique to the adaptive radiation therapy workflow of the brain will provide new opportunities to integrate quantitative imaging relaxometry biomarkers at 1 mm isotropic reconstructed resolution.

title: T-Cell–Derived IFNγ Instructs ECM Crosslinking by Cardiac Fibroblasts Through LOXL3 in Experimental Cardiometabolic HFpEF
authors: Ramona Emig; Zachary L. Robbe; Celina Kley; Sasha A. Smolgovsky; Abraham L. Bayer; Joshua G. Travers; Robert M. Blanton; Timothy A. McKinsey; Lauren Deems Black; Pilar Alcaide
abstract: Abstract Background Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a major clinical challenge characterized by diastolic dysfunction. Left ventricular stiffening and inflammation are hallmarks of HFpEF, yet the contribution of extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffness and the immune–stromal mechanisms driving ECM stiffening in cardiometabolic HFpEF remain poorly understood. Methods We used the murine “2-hit model” of cardiometabolic HFpEF, in which the combination of high fat diet and hypertension induced by L-NAME causes diastolic dysfunction. We evaluated diastolic function by echocardiography and ECM mechanics by uniaxial tensile testing of decellularized cardiac tissue. Functional in vivo studies included genetic depletion of T cells, interferon-γ (IFNγ) knockout mice, and pharmacological lysyl oxidase inhibition. We combined co-cultures of CD4 + T cells and cardiac fibroblasts (CFB) with mechanical testing of cardiac ECM and molecular biology to elucidate cellular and molecular mechanisms. Results Left ventricular ECM stiffness strongly correlated with impaired diastolic function in experimental cardiometabolic HFpEF. Cardiac CD4⁺ T cell infiltration was required for ECM stiffening and upregulation of lysyl oxidase enzymes in CFB. CD4 + T cell-derived IFNγ was both necessary and sufficient to induce LOXL3 in CFB, which increased ECM stiffness in vitro . Mechanistically, IFNγ signaling activated hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF1α) in CFB, driving LOXL3 expression and subsequent collagen crosslinking. Genetic or pharmacologic disruption of this IFNγ–HIF1α–LOXL3 axis in vivo attenuated adverse ECM remodeling and improved diastolic function. Conclusions CD4⁺ T cells promote pathological ECM stiffening in cardiometabolic HFpEF through IFNγ-mediated, LOXL3-dependent ECM crosslinking by CFB. Targeting this immune–stromal pathway may offer a novel therapeutic strategy for HFpEF.

title: Клинико-экономический анализ транскатетерной имплантации в сравнении с хирургической заменой аортального клапана у пациентов низкого риска в Российской Федерации
authors: Огнерубов Дмитрий Викторович; Мершин Кирилл Вячеславович; Курбанов Гамид Магомедсаламович; Берсенева Евгения Александровна; Меркулов Евгений Владимирович
abstract: Проведен клинико-экономический анализ транскатетерной имплантации аортального клапана (ТИАК) в сравнении с хирургической заменой аортального клапана (ХЗАК) у пациентов с тяжелым аортальным стенозом низкого хирургического риска в условиях системы здравоохранения Российской Федерации. Проведено ретроспективное клинико-экономическое моделирование с 5-летним горизонтом. Данные для группы ХЗАК (n = 208) были получены ретроспективно из базы данных одного кардиохирургического центра (ФГБУ “Национальный медицинский исследовательский центр кардиологии им. акад. Е.И. Чазова” Минздрава России, 2019–2024 годы). В связи с отсутствием репрезентативных локальных данных по ТИАК у пациентов низкого риска клинические исходы (летальность, инсульт, повторная госпитализация) для группы ТИАК (n = 496) были взяты из 5-летних результатов исследования PARTNER 3. Экономическая оценка, включавшая анализ коэффициентов “затраты/эффективность” и “затраты/полезность”, проводилась с использованием российских тарифов и дисконтированием затрат (5%). Пятилетняя дисконтированная стоимость ХЗАК составила 1 051 088 руб., ТИАК – 2 149 365 руб. Локальная когорта ХЗАК продемонстрировала лучшие 5-летние клинические исходы по сравнению с данными ТИАК из PARTNER 3, включая более низкую летальность (5,8 против 10,0%), частоту инсультов (1,92 против 5,8%; p = 0,015) и больших кровотечений (2,9 против 10,2%; p = 0,0003). Группа ХЗАК также набрала больше лет жизни с поправкой на качество (quality-adjusted life year, QALY) за 5-летний период (4,14 против 3,88 года). Инкрементный показатель “затраты/полезность” был отрицательным (–4 224 142 руб./QALY), что характеризует ТИАК как доминируемую технологию (более дорогую и менее эффективную). В рамках данной 5-летней модели, основанной на локальных данных ХЗАК и тарифах РФ, ХЗАК является экономически доминирующей стратегией лечения пациентов низкого хирургического риска по сравнению с ТИАК.

title: Integrative multi-omics and machine learning identify mechanical stimulus-related genes and immune microenvironment remodeling in heart failure
authors: Cheng Zhang; Linna Zhao; Jiahuan Sun; Xiaodan Wang; Chuang Zhang; Aiying Li
abstract: Background Heart failure (HF) is a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, driven by complex pathophysiological processes including abnormal mechanical stress and immune microenvironment remodeling. Although mechanical stimulus is known to trigger maladaptive cardiac remodeling, the systematic role of mechanical stimulus-related genes (MSRGs) in HF diagnosis and immune modulation remains poorly defined. This study aims to identify MSRG-based diagnostic biomarkers, characterize molecular subtypes, and explore their cellular localization and immune microenvironment interactions in HF. Methods Bulk transcriptomic data and MSigDB-curated MSRGs were analyzed. Differential expression screening identified MSRGs altered between HF and healthy specimens. Three algorithms—Random Forest, LASSO, and SVM-RFE—were jointly applied to select diagnostic biomarkers and build a nomogram. Consensus clustering defined MSRG-based subtypes, with immune profiles compared across groups. Single-cell sequencing localized key biomarkers in cardiac tissues. A transverse aortic constriction (TAC)-induced rat HF model served for in vivo validation via RT-qPCR, Western blotting, and immunohistochemistry. Results A total of 53 MSRG-related DEGs were identified, from which 11 core diagnostic biomarkers were selected. The nomogram model showed high predictive performance. Consensus clustering revealed two distinct HF subtypes: Cluster A exhibited enhanced metabolic and homeostatic pathways, while Cluster B showed pronounced extracellular matrix remodeling and fibrotic features, with differential immune infiltration. Single-cell analysis demonstrated CASP1 enrichment in macrophages/monocytes and PTN/MDK enrichment in fibroblasts. In vivo validation confirmed significant upregulation of PTN, MDK, and CASP1 at both mRNA and protein levels in TAC hearts, alongside elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-1β) and fibrotic markers, linking mechanical stimulus-related genes to local inflammation and adverse remodeling. Conclusion MSRGs serve as robust diagnostic biomarkers for HF and enable the identification of two molecular subtypes with distinct immune microenvironment and biological pathway profiles. The CASP1-MDK-PTN axis emerges as a potential pathogenic cascade connecting mechanical stress to inflammatory and fibrotic remodeling. These findings provide a framework for early molecular subtyping, improved risk stratification, and targeted immunomodulatory therapy in HF.

title: Distinct Biomarker Signatures of CMR-Defined Myocardial Remodeling in Moderate Aortic Stenosis
authors: Jan M. Wrobel; Jan Paul Janßen; Alina Beckmann; Jasmin Shamekhi; Mohammed Bahaaeldin; Julian Alexander Luetkens; Ibrahim Hawwari; Stephan Nienaber; Bernardo Franklin; Malte Kelm; Georg Nickenig; David C. Maintz; Stephan Ernst Baldus; Tobias Zeus; Lenhard Pennig; Victor Mauri
abstract: Background: Moderate aortic stenosis (AS) is associated with adverse outcomes, yet the myocardial response to pressure overload varies substantially between patients and is incompletely reflected by valve hemodynamics. We aimed to determine whether circulating biomarkers of myocardial stress, injury, and fibrosis associate with cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR)-defined myocardial remodeling in moderate AS. Methods: Eighty-nine patients with moderate AS prospectively underwent CMR (cine imaging, T1 mapping, extracellular volume fraction [ECV], late gadolinium enhancement [LGE]) with concurrent measurement of NT-proBNP, high-sensitivity troponin T, sST2, TIMP-1, and Galectin-3. Biomarker associations with the phenotype-defining CMR parameters were tested with adjustment for age, sex, and renal function and correction for multiple testing, and patients were additionally classified into 4 hierarchical remodeling phenotypes. Results: Six of 20 biomarker-CMR associations remained significant after correction for multiple testing. NT-proBNP tracked LV mass index (beta=0.50), ECV (beta=0.35), and LGE burden (beta=0.43, all q<0.05). TIMP-1 and Galectin-3 were selectively associated with native T1 (both beta=0.35, q=0.012), and sST2 was inversely associated with LV mass index (beta=-0.27, q=0.046). TIMP-1 (adjusted OR 2.18 per SD, 95% CI 1.37-3.48, q=0.005) and NT-proBNP (OR 2.10, 1.19-3.69, q=0.026) increased with higher hierarchical remodeling phenotype. No biomarker was associated with echocardiographic mean gradient, peak velocity, or indexed valve area after correction. Conclusions: Circulating biomarkers showed distinct associations with CMR measures of myocardial remodeling in moderate AS. Matrix-related biomarkers were associated with native T1, whereas NT-proBNP was associated across several remodeling domains. These signals were not measurably related to valve hemodynamics.

title: Diffuse coronary vasospasm causing refractory ventricular fibrillation after minimally invasive mitral valve replacement in a patient with anomalous right coronary artery: a case report
authors: Jie Wu; Tu'erhong Fei'erdun; 路万里
abstract: Malignant arrhythmias and circulatory failure after heart valve surgery are most commonly associated with inadequate myocardial protection, electrolyte disturbances, and prosthetic valve dysfunction. In contrast, isolated diffuse coronary vasospasm is a rare peri-operative complication with substantial risk of life-threatening cardiogenic shock and high early mortality when unrecognized. Anomalous origin of the right coronary artery (RCA) arising from the left coronary sinus represents a rare congenital coronary anatomical variant, which may confer increased susceptibility to peri-operative vasospasm under surgical physiological stress. Furthermore, this abnormal ostial location frequently results in technical difficulty for selective guide-catheter engagement during emergency coronary angiography, limiting local intracoronary vasodilator delivery and rendering pharmacologic management particularly challenging in acute postoperative scenarios. Herein, we report a case of diffuse coronary vasospasm following rheumatic valve surgery in a patient with an anomalous right coronary artery originating from the left coronary sinus, and summarize our diagnostic and therapeutic experience to provide a reference for similar clinical scenarios. A 58-year-old man with a 10-year history of rheumatic heart disease and hypertension was admitted with cough, sputum production, palpitations, and orthopnea. The preoperative diagnoses included rheumatic mitral stenosis, persistent atrial fibrillation, left atrial thrombus, tricuspid regurgitation, and an anomalous RCA arising from the left coronary sinus without significant stenosis. The patient underwent minimally invasive mitral valve replacement along with concomitant procedures. After aortic declamping, he developed ventricular arrhythmias, global myocardial hypokinesia, and failed to wean from cardiopulmonary bypass, requiring venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) support. In the intensive care unit (ICU), recurrent ventricular arrhythmias accompanied by ST-segment elevation were observed. Emergency coronary angiography demonstrated diffuse coronary vasospasm. The spasm in the left coronary system resolved after administration of vasodilators, whereas the anomalous RCA showed a poor response to intracoronary drug therapy. Emergency coronary artery bypass grafting was subsequently performed. The patient recovered uneventfully and was discharged with normal cardiac function. Diffuse coronary vasospasm represents a rare but life-threatening complication following cardiac valve surgery and may lead to refractory circulatory collapse. When this complication occurs in patients with congenital anomalous coronary anatomy, pharmacological therapy is prone to failure due to challenges in targeted intracoronary drug delivery. Timely surgical revascularization should therefore be considered early and may prove life-saving for these high-risk individuals.

title: Ultra-high-resolution Photon-Counting CT for Leaflet-Specific Evaluation of Fibrosis and Calcification in Aortic Stenosis
authors: Mohammed Bahaaeldin; Jasmin Shamekhi; Bernardo S. Franklin; Sebastian Nowak; Alexander M.C. Bohner; Dmitrij Kravchenko; Jan M. Wrobel; Raphael Phinicarides; Lenhard Pennig; Jan Paul Janßen; Carsten Gietzen; Sebastian Zimmer; Stephan Ernst Baldus; Malte Kelm; Georg Nickenig; Tobias Zeus; Victor Mauri; Julian Alexander Luetkens
abstract: Objectives: Ultra-high-resolution photon-counting detector (PCD)-CT may enable leaflet-specific analysis of aortic valve fibrosis and calcification, providing insights into early aortic stenosis (AS) disease progression. This study aimed to investigate how PCD-CT leaflet-specific calcific and fibrotic volumes influence cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) leaflet mobility. Materials and methods: Participants with moderate aortic AS prospectively underwent both PCD-CT (n=80) and CMR (n=58). Using PCD-CT, calcific and fibrotic volumes were segmented for right (RCC), left (LCC), and non-coronary cusps (NCC) and indexed to the aortic annulus area (ICV and IFV). CMR-derived leaflet mobility index (LMI) was assessed. Two raters compared image quality using a Likert scale (1=poor to 5=excellent) and distinguishability of individual leaflets in PCD-CT with EID-CT (n=82). Results: PCD-CT analysis showed that calcification was higher in males (e.g., ICVRCC: 15+/-16 vs. 4+/-7 uL/cm^2; p<0.001), while fibrosis was higher in females (e.g., IFVLCC: 47+/-18 vs. 34+/-15 uL/cm^2; p=0.004) across all leaflets. Fibrocalcific ratio was higher in LCC (53+/-276) compared to RCC (19+/-48; p<0.001) and NCC (13.5+/-34; p<0.001). LMI of RCC was higher in females compared to men (0.66+/-0.21 vs. 0.38+/-0.33; p=0.008). LMILCC and LMINCC showed no sex differences. LMIRCC negatively correlated with ICVRCC (ρ=-0.64 [-0.77, -0.46]; p<0.001) and LMINCC with ICVNCC (ρ=-0.69 [-0.80, -0.53]; p<0.001), whereas LMILCC negatively correlated with IFVLCC (ρ=-0.35 [-0.56, -0.10]; p=0.007), particularly in females (ρ=-0.70 [-0.89, -0.31]; p=0.003). PCD-CT yielded higher image quality (5 [IQR 4-5] vs. 3 [3-4]; p<0.001) and leaflet distinguishability (79/80 [99%] vs. 42/82 [51%]; p<0.001) than EID-CT. Conclusions: Ultra-high-resolution PCD-CT allows for leaflet-specific quantification of indexed fibrotic and calcific volume. These volumes demonstrate sex- and leaflet-specific differences that may distinctly contribute to AS pathophysiology.

title: Long-term clinical and echocardiographic outcomes after mitral valve surgery for severe mitral annular calcification
authors: Yoganiranjana Dharuman; Egan Leonidovich Kalmykov; Mirko Doss
abstract: Objective To assess the long-term clinical and echocardiographic outcomes of mitral valve surgery with annular decalcification and pericardial patch reconstruction in patients with severe mitral annular calcification (MAC). Patients and methods Between 2012 and 2022, 112 consecutive high-risk patients (67 women, 45 men; mean age 66.5 ± 13.6 years) underwent surgery for severe MAC with mitral stenosis and/or regurgitation. Mitral valve repair was performed in 55 patients (49%) and replacement in 57 (51%). Concomitant procedures were performed in 65 patients (58%). Mean follow-up was 97 ± 48 months. Results Early mortality was 6.3% ( n = 7) and late mortality was 23.2% ( n = 26). Survival was 89.3%, 77.2%, and 64.1% at 60, 96, and 144 months, respectively. Freedom from reoperation was 98.3% at 60 months and 93.3% at 96 months. At follow-up, no surviving patient had more than grade III mitral regurgitation. Grade III regurgitation was present in 3 patients (4%), while no patient had grade IV regurgitation. Left atrial diameter, left ventricular end-diastolic diameter, and mean transvalvular gradient were significantly lower than before surgery. Conclusion In this high-risk cohort, annular decalcification and pericardial patch reconstruction provided durable valve function and acceptable long-term survival in patients who survived the perioperative period. Perioperative mortality, however, remained substantial.

title: Outcomes of transcatheter aortic valve implantation using evolut self-expanding valves at Cardiovascular Center – E Hospital
authors: Thao Nguyen Phan; The Huy Nguyen; Hai Son Dam; Đức Ngọc Lý
journal: Tạp chí Phẫu thuật và Tim mạch và Lồng ngực Việt Nam
abstract: Objectives: To evaluate the procedural outcomes, safety, and clinical efficacy of Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation (TAVI) using the Evolut self-expanding valve system in patients with severe aortic stenosis at E Hospital. Methods: A descriptive, longitudinal study was conducted on 21 patients undergoing TAVI from December 2019 to December 2025. Results: The mean age was 72.2 ± 8.3 years; males accounted for 52.4%. Complex characteristics included bicuspid aortic valves (33.3%), degenerated bioprosthetic valves (Valve-in-Valve) (19.0%), and concomitant coronary artery disease requiring Chimney stenting (23.8%). The mean EuroSCORE II was 5.2 ± 1.8%, and the STS Score was 4.1 ± 1.5%. Regarding hemodynamics, the effective orifice area (EOA) increased from 0.65 ± 0.15 cm² to 1.85 ± 0.45 cm²; the mean pressure gradient decreased from 55 ± 12 mmHg to 8.5 ± 3.2 mmHg. The procedural volume increased over time, peaking with 9 cases in 2025. In-hospital mortality was 9.5% (2 cases); both occurred in the early phase (2020 and 2023) associated with highly complex anatomy. Moderate paravalvular leak was observed in 1 case (4.8%), and there were no cases of conduction disorders requiring a permanent pacemaker (0%). No major complications were recorded in the 2024–2025 period. At the 6-month follow-up, left ventricular ejection fraction (EF) improved from 57.38 ± 12.1% to 60.15 ± 9.8%. Conclusion: TAVI using Evolut self-expanding valves is a feasible and effective procedure at E Hospital. Despite initial challenges related to the learning curve, the current protocol has been standardized with high safety outcomes. The role of the Heart Team in patient selection and thorough anatomical assessment is the key factor in improving treatment outcomes.

title: Ultra-high-pitch photon-counting computed tomography (PCCT) versus ultra-high-pitch dual-source computed tomography (DSCT) for coronary artery disease evaluation in transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) patients
authors: Ines Mecking; Marc von der Stück; Eric Corban; Michael Frick; Jörg W. Schröder; Roman Iwa; Christiane Katharina Kuhl; Timm Dirrichs
abstract: Rationale and objectives To compare radiation dose and image quality of coronary artery reconstructions obtained from non–coronary-dedicated transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) planning CT scans using ultra-high-pitch photon-counting CT (PCCT) and ultra-high-pitch energy-integrating detector dual-source CT (EID-DSCT; hereafter referred to as DSCT), including assessment of the feasibility of coronary artery evaluation according to the Coronary Artery Disease Reporting and Data System (CAD-RADS). Materials and methods Retrospective study on consecutive patients with aortic valve stenosis (AS) undergoing contrast-enhanced TAVI planning CT, either PCCT or DSCT between August 2021 and June 2023. CT dose index (CTDI) and dose length product (DLP) were used to calculate the effective radiation dose (eRD). Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) were calculated using standardized region-of-interest (ROI) analysis. Coronary arteries were evaluated by three independent radiologists using 5-point Likert scales followed by a classification according to the CAD-RADS system. Results 187 patients (83 female, median age 82, IQR: 76–84) underwent 190 CT-examinations, 103 PCCT (54.2%) and 87 (45.8%) DSCT. Three patients underwent both PCCT and DSCT for clinical reasons. Mean CTDI and DLP were significantly lower in PCCT compared to DSCT (21.9 vs. 52.8 and 607.9 vs. 906.8, respectively; both p < 0.001), with a correspondingly lower mean effective radiation dose (eRD) in PCCT compared to DSCT (10.3 ± 5.4 mSv vs. 15.4 ± 5.6 mSv, p < 0.001). While both SNR and CNR were lower in PCCT than in DSCT (SNR: 35.28 ± 11.63 in PCCT vs. 45.6 ± 16.3 in DSCT, p < 0.001; CNR: 49.25 ± 13.31 in PCCT vs. 57.42 v ± 22.55 in DSCT, p = 0.004), PCCT outperformed DSCT in every one of the eleven visual image categories. Overall image quality was rated as good or excellent in 71.8% (74/103) of PCCT vs. 19.5% (17/87) of DSCT scans. Coronary reconstructions were rated as good or excellent in 72.8% (75/103) of PCCT vs. 20.7% of DSCT datasets. CAD-RADS [1–5] rating was possible in 68.9% (71/103) of PCCT vs. 39.1% (34/87) of DSCT datasets. Conclusion Photon-counting computed tomography (PCCT) allows for significantly improved assessability of the coronary arteries in TAVI planning CT compared with dual-source CT (DSCT), while achieving a substantially lower radiation dose.

title: From TAVR to SAVR
authors: Karen Hovsepyan; Amy Hutchinson; Michael Finamore; Lucas Henn
journal: Translation The University of Toledo Journal of Medical Sciences
abstract: Background:Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is an established minimally invasive therapy for severe aortic stenosis, with a steadily declining incidence of procedural complications. Nevertheless, emergent conversion to surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR), although rare, remains associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Case Summary:A 71-year-old male with severe aortic stenosis and multiple comorbidities underwent elective transfemoral TAVR using a 26-mm SAPIEN 3 Ultra Resilia valve. Initial post-deployment imaging demonstrated satisfactory valve position and hemodynamic performance. On postoperative day 0, the patient developed severe hypertension followed by embolization of the bioprosthetic valve into the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT), resulting in obstruction and interference with the mitral valve apparatus. Given the risk of hemodynamic collapse, the patient was taken emergently for explant of the TAVR . Intraoperative findings revealed a migrated and rotated transcatheter valve causing partial LVOT obstruction and laceration of the ventricular side of the anterior mitral valve leaflet. The valve was successfully explanted, and surgical aortic valve replacement was performed. The postoperative course was complicated by transient acute kidney injury, which resolved prior to discharge on postoperative day 9. Conclusion:This case illustrates a rare but life-threatening complication of TAVR requiring emergent surgical intervention and highlights the importance of vigilant monitoring, strict hemodynamic control, and immediate surgical readiness.

title: From Reduced Order Models to ATLAS: A Real‐Time Platform for Hemodynamics
authors: Zahra Mirzaiyan; Davide Oberto; Pierfrancesco Siena; Gianluigi Rozza
abstract: ABSTRACT Cardiovascular diseases represent one of the leading causes of death worldwide, leading to the development of advanced research in numerical analysis to create decision‐support tools for the clinical community. The main objective is to develop advanced numerical frameworks for accurate diagnosis and personalized treatment planning. While high‐fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations provide detailed hemodynamic insights, their high computational cost, due to the large number of degrees of freedom and complex morphologies involved, limits their use in real‐time clinical routine. Reduced order models (ROMs) have emerged as a powerful framework to overcome these limitations by providing accurate approximations at a significantly reduced computational cost. In this paper, we provide a high‐level overview of the main ROM methodological categories, including linear and nonlinear approaches, and refer to relevant literature for more comprehensive treatments. Despite their potential, the technical complexity and specialized expertise required to implement these methods often hinder their direct application in clinical settings. To overcome these limitations, we introduce ATLAS, a cloud‐native open‐access platform designed to bridge the gap between complex numerical modeling and clinical practice through an intuitive web interface. The potential of the platform is demonstrated through a case study on the left atrial appendage (LAA), focusing on blood stasis as a key indicator of stroke risk. Finally, we discuss the role of ROMs as a key enabling technology for the development of cardiovascular digital twins, highlighting the potential for bidirectional communication between physical patients and their virtual counterparts.

title: Study protocol for a prospective multicenter longitudinal cohort study on progression of moderate aortic valve stenosis, the MODAS Study
authors: Raphael Phinicarides; Kathrin Klein; Christian Jung; Bernardo S. Franklin; Ibrahim Hawwari; Victor Mauri; Jan M. Wrobel; Stephan E. Baldus; Julian A. Luetkens; Jasmin Shamekhi; Georg Nickenig; Verena Veulemans; Malte Kelm; Tobias Zeus
abstract: Background: Calcific aortic stenosis (AS) is one of the most common and prognostically relevant valvular heart diseases, with a growing global burden driven by population ageing. Prediction of disease progression from moderate to severe AS, which would be instrumental for earlier diagnosis and treatment, remains challenging. At the same time, moderate AS is increasingly recognized as a heterogeneous condition associated with clinically relevant risk, particularly in patients with cardiac damage, heart failure, or rapid disease progression. Conventional echocardiographic parameters incompletely capture the biological heterogeneity underlying AS progression. The MODAS study was established to investigate biomarkers and mechanisms of AS progression and outcome using longitudinal multimodal phenotyping. Methods: The MODAS Study is a prospective, multicenter, longitudinal observational cohort study enrolling adults with moderate calcific tricuspid AS at three tertiary heart valve centers in Germany. Participants undergo standardized baseline assessment including clinical phenotyping, laboratory testing, electrocardiography, transthoracic echocardiography, cardiac computed tomography and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging. Biospecimens are collected for biomarker, immunologic, proteomic, and genetic analyses, including genome-wide association studies and assessment of clonal haematopoiesis. Participants are followed annually for up to 5 years with repeat clinical assessment, laboratory testing, and echocardiography. The primary endpoint is time to progression to severe AS according to 2025 ESC/EACTS guideline criteria or aortic valve replacement for severe AS, adjudicated by the local multidisciplinary Heart Team. Secondary endpoints include all-cause mortality and additional clinical outcome trajectories. Multimodal data integration will be used to develop and validate prediction models for disease progression and outcome. Discussion: The MODAS Study will provide a harmonized, deeply phenotyped longitudinal dataset to improve risk stratification in moderate AS and to identify imaging, inflammatory, and genetic markers associated with rapid progression and adverse outcomes. The study is designed to support future personalized surveillance strategies, improved selection for earlier intervention, and mechanistic understanding of calcific AS progression. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05851209 . Registered on 9 May 2023.

title: Anesthetic management of an infant with arterial tortuosity syndrome undergoing combined laparoscopic procedures: a case report
authors: Zainab Alzayer
abstract: Background Arterial tortuosity syndrome (ATS) is a rare autosomal recessive connective-tissue disorder marked by elongation and tortuosity of major arteries, predisposing affected patients to aneurysm formation, stenosis, and arterial dissection. These vascular abnormalities, together with characteristic craniofacial and connective-tissue features, pose significant anesthetic challenges, particularly in airway management, hemodynamic control, and perioperative cardiovascular risk. The complexity is further heightened in infants undergoing prolonged laparoscopic procedures, in which pneumoperitoneum, reverse-Trendelenburg positioning, and the limited physiological reserve of early infancy may adversely affect ventilation, venous return, and cardiovascular stability. Case presentation We describe the anesthetic management of a 3-month-old, 4.6-kg infant with genetically confirmed ATS, who underwent combined laparoscopic repair of a Morgagni diaphragmatic hernia and a para-esophageal hiatal hernia. Preoperative evaluation demonstrated tortuosity of the aorta, head and neck vessels, and pulmonary arteries, without pulmonary hypertension or ventricular dysfunction. Inhalational induction with sevoflurane was performed while preserving spontaneous ventilation because of the anticipated difficult airway and the presence of a Morgagni diaphragmatic hernia, where positive-pressure ventilation could result in gastric insufflation and further distension of herniated abdominal contents. Tracheal intubation was successfully achieved with a 3.0-mm cuffed endotracheal tube. Anesthesia was maintained with sevoflurane and opioid supplementation. Carbon dioxide pneumoperitoneum was introduced gradually, with intra-abdominal pressure maintained below 10 mmHg to limit hemodynamic and ventilatory disturbances. The intraoperative course remained stable, and the patient was extubated uneventfully before transfer to the pediatric intensive care unit. Conclusion This case underscores essential anesthetic considerations for infants with ATS undergoing prolonged laparoscopic procedures, emphasizing anticipatory airway planning, vascular-protective strategies, controlled pneumoperitoneum, vigilant cardiovascular management, and coordinated multidisciplinary care.

title: Sex differences in clinical phenotypes and prognostic associations in acute heart failure
authors: Georgios Aletras; Maria Bachlitzanaki; Stylianos Fiflis; Eirini Bachlitzanaki; Eleni Eleftheriadou; Yannis Pantazis; Emmanuel Foukarakis; Michalis Hamilos; Kostas Stylianou
abstract: Background Women are under-represented in heart failure trials, and the risk markers used in acute heart failure (AHF) derive largely from male-predominant cohorts. In this study, we compared the metabolic, inflammatory, and renal profiles of men and women hospitalized for AHF and tested whether the prognostic value of these markers differs by sex. Methods We analyzed 530 consecutive patients from a prospective single-center AHF registry. Postdischarge mortality was modeled by Cox regression in the 503 patients discharged alive; each of eight covariates was tested for a sex interaction, and 19 metabolic, inflammatory, and renal markers were screened for effect modification by sex. Results The total number of male patients was 284 (53.6%). Women were older (82 vs. 79 years) than men and more often had preserved ejection fraction (65.9% vs. 35.9%), frailty (74.0% vs. 59.9%), and chronic kidney disease; they had a higher total cholesterol level (139 vs. 126 mg/dL), a lower troponin level, a higher E/e′ ratio within preserved ejection fraction, and a lower ferritin level (42 vs. 71 ng/mL; below 100 ng/mL in 76.8% vs. 63.7%). Men more often had an ischemic etiology (45.8% vs. 15.0%), although coronary anatomy was more often unassessed in women (all p < 0.05). In-hospital (5.3% vs. 4.9%) and postdischarge mortality rates (23.6% vs. 26.7%) and renal outcomes did not differ; after full adjustment, male sex was associated with higher postdischarge mortality [hazard ratio (HR) 1.51, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.03–2.22], but this depended on the inclusion of the left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) category. No covariate showed significant effect modification by sex (all p for interaction ≥0.06), with similar optimism-corrected C-indices (men 0.683, women 0.687). Among the 19 markers, only uric acid showed an interaction (women HR 1.15 per mg/dL, 95% CI 1.00–1.33; men 0.91, 0.80–1.03; p = 0.008), not surviving multiplicity correction. Conclusions Men and women hospitalized for AHF are clinically and biochemically distinct populations. Unadjusted mortality rates were similar in both sexes; an adjusted association with male sex was sensitive to the inclusion of the LVEF category and therefore should be interpreted cautiously. No robust sex-related effect modification was found; given the limited number of events, this represents the absence of evidence rather than evidence of similar prognostic associations between the sexes. Low ferritin levels, frequent in women, warrants assessment with complete iron indices; the uric acid interaction is hypothesis-generating.

title: Myocardial remodelling during sacubitril/valsartan therapy in patients with chronic heart failure.
authors: DAVID TABUKASHVILI; V. Kapetivadze; Tamar Lazashvili; Zviadi Maglaperidze
abstract: Abstract: The aim of the study was to identify differences between aliskiren and sacubitril/valsartan in their ability to influence cardiac remodelling, metabolic balance, neurohumoral activation, and clinical symptom severity. A comparative assessment of the clinical effectiveness and impact on the structural and functional state of the myocardium was conducted for two therapeutic strategies in patients with chronic heart failure in Georgia over a 12-month follow-up. The results demonstrated fundamentally different trajectories of therapeutic response. In the sacubitril/valsartan group, early clinical improvement was observed by 6 months, including significant reductions in systolic blood pressure (-6.2%, p<0.001), respiratory rate (-4.5%, p<0.001), and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide levels (-10.0%, p<0.05), along with improved oxygen saturation (+3.5%, p<0.001). Left ventricular ejection fraction increased significantly already at 6 months (from 34.2±4.7% to 37.4±4.0%, p<0.001) and further at 12 months (40.5±3.5%, p<0.001), accompanied by rapid improvement in New York Heart Association functional class, with 9.3% of patients achieving New York Heart Association I by study end. In contrast, the aliskiren group exhibited slower but more pronounced structural reverse remodelling. Significant reductions in left ventricular end-systolic volume (-15.8%, p=0.009), end-diastolic volume (-17.6%, p=0.016), and end-systolic diameter (p=0.002) were observed only at 12 months, along with a modest but significant increase in ejection fraction (p=0.030). Regression of functional mitral and tricuspid regurgitation and a significant decrease in pulmonary artery systolic pressure (-19.7%, p<0.05) were more prominent in this group. Both therapies led to significant improvements in carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, including reductions in glycated haemoglobin, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and triglycerides (p<0.05 for all), indicating a favourable systemic metabolic effect. Overall, findings suggest that sacubitril/valsartan may be preferable when rapid clinical stabilization is required, whereas aliskiren may represent an effective therapeutic option for patients with advanced structural cardiac remodelling.

title: Beyond the lungs and heart: a possible association between digestive disease and exercise intolerance in 10 dogs
authors: Alexandra Corsaletti; Michael Martineau; Hugues Etien; Kévin Le Boedec
abstract: Introduction Exercise intolerance and panting are classically attributed to cardiac, respiratory, or other diseases. In some cases, the underlying etiology remains undetermined despite a comprehensive diagnostic workup. While fatigue is one of the most common symptoms in humans with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), chronic enteropathy is not currently recognized as a primary cause of exercise intolerance in dogs. Methods A retrospective review was conducted on the medical records of 10 dogs presenting with exercise intolerance lacking overt digestive or respiratory signs. All dogs underwent empirical gastrointestinal-directed medical and dietary therapies with subsequent owner-perceived clinical resolution. Results Ten dogs presenting with chronic exercise intolerance were evaluated. Six of these dogs also exhibited unexplained panting at rest (6/10). Subtle gastrointestinal signs and abdominal discomfort on palpation were present in four and five cases, respectively. Standard cardiopulmonary and metabolic investigations were largely unremarkable. Notably, half of the cohort (5/10) exhibited cobalamin insufficiency or deficiency. Dogs were managed with gastrointestinal-directed medical therapies (e.g., prokinetics, acid suppressants, tylosin) and/or dietary modifications (predominantly low-fat, single-protein (monoprotein), or hydrolyzed diets). Following these targeted interventions, all dogs achieved complete clinical resolution per owners within a median of 21 days. Conclusion A gastrointestinal etiology may be considered in dogs presenting with unexplained exercise intolerance and excessive panting. Subtle physical exam findings, serum cobalamin and folate concentrations, and empirical dietary/medical trials can be used to support clinical suspicion. This case series suggests a potential canine equivalent of human IBD-related fatigue, highlighting the need for further research into the gut-brain axis, intestinal dysbiosis, and delayed gastric emptying in veterinary medicine.

title: Fulminant Disseminated Gonococcal Infection Complicated by Meningitis, Endocarditis, and Septic Shock in an Immunocompetent Young Woman: A Case Report
authors: Abdul  Mashood Madni; Mujtaba Ali Hasan
abstract: Disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) is an uncommon but potentially life-threatening complication of Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection caused by hematogenous dissemination from mucosal sites. The classical manifestations of DGI include dermatitis, tenosynovitis, and migratory polyarthritis. Severe invasive complications such as meningitis, endocarditis, septic shock, and multiorgan failure are rare.An 18-year-old immunocompetent woman with no significant past medical history presented to the infectious diseases ward with fever and severe suprapubic pain. On admission, her temperature was 38.2°C, blood pressure was 130/85 mmHg, heart rate was 80 beats/min, respiratory rate was 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. Physical examination revealed multiple painful pustular and hemorrhagic bullous lesions measuring approximately 1 mm over the elbows, along with clinical evidence of tenosynovitis.Microbiological investigations confirmed disseminated gonococcal infection, with N. gonorrhoeae isolated from vaginal swab, blood, and synovial fluid cultures. Concurrent Chlamydia trachomatis infection was identified. Treatment was initiated with intravenous ceftriaxone (1 g once daily) and oral doxycycline (100 mg twice daily). Despite antimicrobial therapy, the patient developed polyarthritis on hospital day 5, mitral valve endocarditis on day 7, severe hepatic dysfunction on day 8, and acute kidney injury and meningitis on day 9. Cerebrospinal fluid culture subsequently confirmed N. gonorrhoeae. On day 10, she developed septic shock requiring intensive care admission and norepinephrine support. Seizures developed on day 11, and the patient died on day 12 from septic shock secondary to disseminated gonococcal infection with multiorgan failure.This case illustrates a rare, fulminant presentation of DGI with progressive involvement of the skin, musculoskeletal system, cardiovascular system, central nervous system, and multiple organs. Early recognition of characteristic DGI manifestations, prompt microbiological investigation, and timely initiation of appropriate antimicrobial therapy are essential components of management.

title: Late Entrant in a PMA-Only Category: Regulatory Strategy and Project Management for a Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Valve Repair System
authors: Anushree Siddharth Sheladia; Peivand Pirouzi
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: First-in-class devices attract most attention in regulatory strategy discussions, but a representative transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) system illustrates the more common case of a follower device: by the time a second entrant pursues US approval in an already-established therapeutic category, an incumbent has typically already shaped clinical practice patterns, reimbursement structures, and physician familiarity. This article reconstructs the generalized regulatory journey of a TEER system of this kind from classification through post-market surveillance, distinguishing documented regulatory facts from the author's own strategic analysis. The article addresses the classification rationale across three jurisdictions, the pivotal trial design choice between a single-arm and a randomized head-to-head comparison, the asymmetry between US and European Union indications for a device of this kind, and the distinct reimbursement and market-access dynamics in the United States and Canada. The article closes with recommendations for regulatory affairs professionals developing a late-entrant strategy in an established, single-pathway device category.Keywords: transcatheter edge-to-edge repair; mitral regurgitation; follower device strategy; Premarket Approval; Health Canada Class IV; EU MDR; regulatory artificial intelligence

title: Mid-term Outcomes of Minimally Invasive Mitral Valve Repair Using Valve-Preserving Techniques for Severe Mitral Regurgitation due to Barlow’s Disease
authors: Công Hiếu Lương; Hoang Dinh Nguyen; Tho Tuan Anh Pham; Minh Bao Luan Tran
journal: Tạp chí Phẫu thuật và Tim mạch và Lồng ngực Việt Nam
abstract: Introduction: Barlow’s disease is a form of degenerative mitral valve disease characterized by lesions involving multiple scallops of the mitral leaflets, making surgical repair technically complex and challenging. In such cases, mitral valve repair using valve-preserving techniques through a minimally invasive approach offers several advantages for patients. However, data regarding the mid-term outcomes of minimally invasive mitral valve repair using valve-preserving techniques in Barlow’s disease remain limited. Therefore, this study was conducted to evaluate these outcomes. Methods: This retrospective cohort study included all patients with severe mitral regurgitation due to Barlow’s disease who underwent minimally invasive mitral valve repair using valve-preserving techniques at the University Medical Center Ho Chi Minh City from 2020 to 2024. Patients were followed up continuously for a period ranging from 6 months to 5 years. Results: A total of 26 patients with severe mitral regurgitation due to Barlow’s disease underwent minimally invasive mitral valve repair using valve-preserving techniques. The mean follow-up duration was 29.9 ± 19.8 months. During follow-up, no mortality or reoperation was observed. Three patients (11.5%) developed moderate mitral regurgitation, while the remaining patients had either no regurgitation or only mild mitral regurgitation. Conclusion: Minimally invasive mitral valve repair for Barlow’s disease using valve-preserving techniques demonstrated favorable mid-term outcomes, with a low rate of recurrent moderate or greater mitral regurgitation and no cases requiring reoperation.

title: The Mitral Valve Heart Team 2.0: Integrating Imaging, Surgery, Transcatheter Therapies and Artificial Intelligence
authors: Salvatore Poddi; Alessio Rungatscher
journal: Journal of Cardiovascular Development and Disease
abstract: The management of mitral valve disease is rapidly evolving, driven by advances in multimodality imaging, surgical techniques, transcatheter therapies, and artificial intelligence (AI). In this changing landscape, the traditional Heart Team model should evolve toward a more integrated and dynamic multidisciplinary approach. The “Mitral Valve Heart Team 2.0” may combine detailed anatomical and functional characterization with surgical expertise, transcatheter treatment options, and AI-assisted data integration to support individualized treatment strategies. Advanced imaging increasingly informs not only diagnosis but also procedural planning and patient selection, while AI may improve reproducibility of mitral regurgitation assessment, risk stratification, and phenotypic characterization. However, these technologies should augment rather than replace expert clinical judgment and shared decision-making. This Communication discusses the emerging components of this paradigm and proposes a practical framework in which imaging specialists, surgeons, interventional cardiologists, heart failure specialists, and data-driven tools interact throughout the patient pathway. The objective is not to create a larger Heart Team, but a more integrated one, capable of matching the right patient to the right treatment at the right time.

title: Long-term myocardial deformation abnormalities and biomarker associations in pediatric myopericarditis: a speckle-tracking echocardiographic study
authors: Şule Arıcı; Selen Karagözlü; Elif Erolu Kibris; Figen Akalın
abstract: Background and objectives Subclinical myocardial deformation abnormalities may be detectable during long-term follow-up in pediatric patients with a history of myopericarditis despite apparently normal conventional echocardiographic findings. This study aimed to comprehensively evaluate long-term myocardial deformation abnormalities using speckle-tracking echocardiography and to assess their associations with acute-phase inflammatory and cardiac biomarkers. Methods Thirty pediatric patients with a history of myopericarditis and 22 age- and sex-matched healthy controls were included. Acute-phase clinical, laboratory, electrocardiographic, and echocardiographic data were retrospectively collected. At long-term follow-up, comprehensive echocardiographic evaluation including tissue Doppler imaging and speckle-tracking–derived longitudinal and circumferential strain analysis was prospectively performed. Associations between acute-phase biomarkers and long-term echocardiographic findings were analyzed. Results At a mean follow-up of 32.8 ± 12.0 months, patients demonstrated significantly reduced global longitudinal strain (−12.43 ± 6.67% vs. −17.77 ± 1.94%, p < 0.001) and global circumferential strain (−16.04 ± 12.50% vs. −25.14 ± 4.73%, p = 0.002) compared with controls despite largely preserved conventional systolic function. Segmental longitudinal and circumferential strain parameters were also impaired, accompanied by increased time-to-peak strain dispersion. Higher neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio and systemic immune-inflammation index values correlated with less negative global longitudinal strain values, while CRP correlated with impaired global circumferential strain. Conclusions Pediatric patients with a history of myopericarditis may exhibit subclinical myocardial deformation abnormalities at long-term follow-up despite apparently preserved conventional echocardiographic findings. Speckle-tracking echocardiography may provide incremental value for detecting subtle myocardial deformation abnormalities beyond conventional systolic assessment. Exploratory associations were observed between acute-phase inflammatory biomarkers and long-term myocardial deformation parameters; however, larger prospective studies are needed to clarify whether these findings have causal or clinical significance.

title: Successful transcatheter treatment of chronic mechanical haemolysis after cardiac surgery: a case report
authors: Nico Schupp; Thushiha Logeswaran; Marius Rohde; Hakan Akintürk; Christian Jux
abstract: Chronic haemolysis is a rare but important postsurgical complication in children with congenital heart defects. A 13-year-old with a previously uncorrected complex heart defect underwent corrective surgery. He developed haemolysis postoperatively. A mechanical cause due to turbulent flow through a narrowed intraventricular Dacron patch tunnel was suspected. Balloon dilatation and stent placement successfully resolved the stenosis and haemolysis.

title: Elevated Doppler-estimated right ventricular systolic pressure in complete atrioventricular block and its response to atrioventricular-synchronous pacing
authors: Byeng-Ju Son; Sungyun Jung; Byung-Jun Kim; Hong-Ju Kim; Hyongjun Kim
abstract: Background Complete atrioventricular block causes both bradycardia and loss of atrioventricular synchrony. Case reports have described marked elevations in Doppler-estimated right ventricular systolic pressure that fall after pacing, but the prevalence and consistency of this phenotype have not been examined in a cohort. Methods We retrospectively studied consecutive patients in sinus rhythm with complete atrioventricular block and a left ventricular ejection fraction of at least 50%, identified from 142 permanent pacemaker implantations at one center between 2021 and 2026. Right atrial pressure was estimated using current guideline categories. The prespecified primary endpoint was the paired change in Doppler-estimated right ventricular systolic pressure between the native state and the first study within 72 h of atrioventricular-synchronous pacing. Tricuspid regurgitant signal quality was graded on envelope completeness and analyzed alongside it. Results Thirty patients formed the native cohort and 14 had paired studies. Doppler-estimated right ventricular systolic pressure was 44.0 mmHg (interquartile range 32.4–50.3) during native block and was 35 mmHg or greater in 21 patients. In the paired cohort it fell from 46.6 to 25.0 mmHg in all 14 patients (median relative change −51.4%; P < 0.001), and the proportion with values of 35 mmHg or greater fell from 11 to 3 ( P = 0.008). Both the tricuspid regurgitant gradient and the estimated right atrial pressure decreased, and tricuspid regurgitation grade fell in 7 patients and increased in none. Paced QRS duration increased, and the heart-rate change was not correlated with the change in Doppler-estimated right ventricular systolic pressure. Signal quality tended to decline after pacing; in a post hoc analysis restricted to the 7 patients in whom it was unchanged or improved, the reduction persisted (median relative change −33.8%; P = 0.016). In four catheterized patients, Doppler estimates diverged from invasive pressures in both directions. Conclusion Elevated Doppler-estimated right ventricular systolic pressure was common during complete atrioventricular block and fell consistently after atrioventricular-synchronous pacing. Because signal quality changed concurrently and invasive pressure did not invariably track the estimate, the magnitude of the observed Doppler reduction, and whether pulmonary artery pressure itself falls, remain uncertain.

title: Successful repair of an ebstein-like malformation of the mitral valve: a case report
authors: Sinh Hien Nguyen; Dang Hung Nguyen; Huu Phong Nguyen
journal: Tạp chí Phẫu thuật và Tim mạch và Lồng ngực Việt Nam
abstract: Background: Ebstein-like malformation of the mitral valve is an exceptionally rare congenital anomaly characterized by incomplete delamination and apical displacement of the posterior mitral leaflet. The resulting deficiency of functional leaflet tissue may cause severe mitral regurgitation and poses a major challenge for valve repair. Case presentation: A 9-year-old boy presented with fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Echocardiography showed severe mitral regurgitation, marked posterior leaflet hypoplasia, and left atrial enlargement. Intraoperatively, the posterior leaflet was almost completely adherent to the ventricular wall, and the posterior annulus was poorly defined, apically displaced, and dilated. The anterior leaflet and its subvalvular apparatus were preserved. The posterior leaflet and chordal structures were reconstructed using glutaraldehyde-treated autologous pericardium, followed by prosthetic ring annuloplasty. Intraoperative echocardiography demonstrated competent valve closure without mitral stenosis or systolic anterior motion. The postoperative course was uneventful, and mitral valve function remained stable at the one-month follow-up. Conclusion: Reconstruction of the posterior leaflet and chordal structures using autologous pericardium, combined with ring annuloplasty, may provide a valve-preserving option for pediatric patients with an Ebstein-like malformation of the mitral valve when the anterior leaflet and its corresponding subvalvular apparatus are adequately preserved; although long-term follow-up is required to assess durability

title: Distinct patterns of vascular failure in COL1A1-associated osteogenesis imperfecta and FBN1-associated Marfan syndrome
authors: Hiroshi Kubota; Hidehito Endo; Masao Nunokawa; Toshihiko Isaji; Sachito Minegishi; Hiroshi Tsuchiya; Masaru Kimura; Toru Ikezoe; Yusuke Inaba; Yu Takahashi; Kouta Kogure; Tomohiro Iwakura; Yaeko Ichikawa; Yutaka Hosoi
abstract: Introduction Heritable connective tissue disorders are an important cause of aortic disease; however, the mechanisms of vascular failure in genetically defined aortopathies remain incompletely understood. Methods We analyzed the clinical course, imaging findings, and histopathologic features of two patients with clinically and genetically characterized connective tissue disorders: COL1A1-associated osteogenesis imperfecta and FBN1-associated Marfan syndrome. Results The COL1A1-associated patient developed multilevel arterial complications, including aortic regurgitation requiring aortic valve replacement at age 36, rupture of a dissected right common iliac artery in the same year, chronic type A aortic dissection requiring root, ascending, and arch replacement at age 54, and rupture of the infrarenal abdominal aorta at a diameter of only 30 mm. The FBN1-associated patient presented with type B aortic dissection at age 34 and subsequently developed progressive aneurysmal disease requiring staged thoracoabdominal replacement, total arch replacement for acute type A dissection, and aortic root replacement, followed by multiple peripheral vascular reconstructions. Histopathologic examination demonstrated valvular myxomatous degeneration in both cases. The aortic wall in both patients showed medial degeneration with fragmentation of elastic fibers. In addition, the COL1A1-associated patient demonstrated abdominal aortic wall thinning, with a minimum thickness of 1.25 mm. Conclusions These two patients exhibited contrasting longitudinal vascular courses despite some overlapping histopathologic findings. The COL1A1-associated OI patient experienced rupture of a dissected infrarenal aortic segment, whereas the FBN1-associated Marfan patient experienced repeated dissections followed by progressive vascular dilatation and multiple surgical reconstructions. These observations are descriptive and do not establish genotype-specific patterns or mechanisms of vascular failure.

title: Editorial: Management of arrhythmias in acute and intensive care settings
authors: Martin Balík; Štěpán Havránek
abstract: Cardiac arrhythmias become frequent in general population which transmits to the incidence among the critically ill. (1) As an independent mortality predictor, they represent either a primary problem or consequence of the underlying critical illness and an important driver of further hemodynamic deterioration. (2,3) The evidence in critical care arrhythmia management is limited because some of the conclusions generated on large cohorts of cardiology outpatients cannot be applied in the acute and intensive care setting. Hence, the decisions are often driven by available bedside imaging and applied physiology. (4) Shortened diastolic filling, loss of atrial contribution, irregular ventricular activation, increased myocardial oxygen demand, reduced coronary perfusion, and impaired ventricular function may all contribute to a rapid decline in cardiac output, particularly in patients with pre-existing ventricular dysfunction or limited cardiovascular reserve. (5,6) The resulting hypotension and congestion, sympathetic activation and myocardial ischemia in turn facilitate recurrent arrhythmia. Thus, a self-perpetuating cycle may develop in which arrhythmia aggravates hemodynamic compromise, while hemodynamic and metabolic deterioration further increases arrhythmogenicity. (5)(6)(7) Potentially reversible precipitants-including acute myocardial ischemia, electrolyte abnormalities, acidosis, hypoxemia, elevated filling pressure, infection, drug toxicity, and proarrhythmic medication-must be identified and corrected simultaneously.
